title: Africa’s green industrialization reality check: skills follow demand
body:
We often blame Africa’s limited green industrialization on skill shortages. But that’s only part of the story.

Increasingly, the continent is not short of training programs. What it is short of is demand that sticks.

Skills—engineers, technicians, grid managers, maintenance crews, applied R&D—do not appear in a vacuum. They emerge when firms have orders to fill, contracts to honor, and markets to serve.

Conder these scenarios.

Scenario 1: Train First, Hope Later

- Africa trains engineers, technicians, and renewable-energy graduates—often at scale. However, demand is fragmented, projects are sporadic and manufacturing orders are thin or uncertain.
- The result: Skills migrate or shift sectors, firms underinvest in upgrading, and local R&D floats above production

**Implication:** Africa ends up exporting skills and minerals, while importing finished green technologies.

Scenario 2: Projects Without Industrial Anchors

- Solar parks, wind farms, and pilot hydrogen projects multiply but each is negotiated in isolation. There is no aggregated demand, no industrial anchor.
- The result: Limited learning-by-doing, weak local supply chains, and firms have no reason build long-term training pipelines

**Implication:** Green industrialization looks active and busy but the industrial base stays shallow.

Scenario 3: Demand-Led Green Industrialization

- Governments do the hard work, coordinating energy, mining, industry, and trade policy. Demand is made visible and credible.
- The result: Offtake agreements give firms confidence to invest in skills; Anchor buyers (fertilizer, steel, cement, agro-processing) absorb green power and inputs at scale; Public procurement creates early markets for local production

Here, skills emerge because markets exist.

Scenario 3 is the only path where Africa stops being just a site of extraction and installation and becomes a site of production, learning, and upgrading.

The lesson is simple, but uncomfortable: Skills do not lead demand. Demand pulls skills into existence

The real question is no longer whether Africa have the technology or skills?” It is whether it has the coordinated markets—national and regional—that allow skills to take root?”

This is the real industrial test of the green industrialization in Africa.

Green industrialization happens when markets, skills, and production grow together. This is where the AfCFTA becomes quintessential for Africa’s green industrialization.

Elvis K. Avenyo (Ph.D.) Victor Osei Kwadwo, Ph.D.Solomon Owusu Woubet Kassa, PhD Rex Asiama (PhD)
